Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). 1	# kolosok-rehack — AI Development Guidelines
2	
3	Team **Kolosok** at the **European Hackathon League (EHL) Grand Finale**, Munich (TUM.ai).
4	This file is the rulebook for every AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, …) and human working in this repo.
5	**Read it fully before your first change.** Human setup (GitHub token, credentials) lives in `README-Human`.
6	
7	Source: [EHL Finale – All you need to know](https://tum-ai.notion.site/REDACTED)
8	
9	---
10	
11	## 0. Hard rules (non-negotiable)
12	
13	1. **Entire must be enabled and every commit must carry a checkpoint.** The organisers will reject a submission that does not use Entire. No Entire → no valid submission.
14	2. **All work goes through git and gets pushed to `origin`.** Nothing that exists only on one laptop counts.
15	3. **`main` must always be demo-able.** We have a strict 6-minute slot for pitch + demo + questions.
16	4. **Never commit secrets** (API keys, tokens, `.env`). Entire redacts secrets in session logs, but do not rely on that.
17	5. **Never rewrite pushed history** (no `push --force`, no amending/rebasing pushed commits, no deleting `entire/*` branches or refs). Checkpoints are tied to commits; rewriting history can orphan them.
18	
19	## 1. Key times (Munich local time)
20	
21	| When | What |
22	|---|---|
23	| Sat 10 Oct, 11:00–11:30 | Entire technical onboarding |
24	| **Sat 10 Oct, 13:00** | **Challenge selection deadline** (captain, on https://ehl.gg/) |
25	| Sat 13:30 → Sun 12:00 | Hacking |
26	| **Sun 11 Oct, 12:00** | **Submission deadline** — hard stop |
27	| Sun 12:00–14:30 | Challenge pitches (6 min incl. Q&A) |
28	| Sun 15:30–16:30 | Main-stage final (6 teams) |
29	
30	Internal targets: **feature freeze Sun 10:00**, first full submission by **Sun 10:30**, final re-submission by **11:45**.
31	Submissions can be repeated as often as we like before the deadline, so submit early and update.
32	
33	**Challenge:** BMW Group — AI for Product Decision Making: an app that turns customer feedback, product/sales data and web research into prioritized, PM-reviewed customer requirements with a full audit trail. Details: [`BMW-Challenge.md`](BMW-Challenge.md).
34	
35	## 2. Setup checklist (each machine, once)
36	
37	Prerequisites: `git` on `PATH` (Entire shells out to it — it fails with `exec: "git": executable file not found` otherwise).
38	
39	```bash
40	# 1. Install Entire (bash / Git Bash). On Windows the binary ends up in ~/.local/bin/entire.exe
41	curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash
42	
43	# 2. On the main branch of this repo:
44	git checkout main && git pull
45	git config pull.rebase true      # plain `git pull` makes merge commits, which carry no checkpoint
46	entire login                     # if not logged in yet
47	entire enable                    # enables session tracking in this repo
48	entire agent add claude-code     # install hooks for your agent; `entire agent list` shows others (codex, cursor, …)
49	
50	# 3. Verify
51	entire status
52	entire doctor                    # if anything looks off
53	```
54	
55	**You are set up correctly when** your next commit prints:
56	
57	```
58	[entire] Pushing 1 checkpoint ref(s) to origin.... done
59	```
60	
61	If you don't see that line, stop and fix Entire before writing more code.
62	
63	## 3. Git workflow
64	
65	- **Commit small and often** — at least every meaningful step, ideally every 15–30 min of agent work. Each commit becomes a checkpoint linking the code to the prompt/reasoning behind it.
66	- **Commit only from within a tracked agent session**, after the agent made the change with its file-edit tools. Hand-made commits, merge commits and shell (`sed`, `echo >`) edits get no checkpoint.
67	- **After every commit** check the checkpoint is there: `git log -1 --format=%B` must show an `Entire-Checkpoint:` line. If it is missing, fix it *before* pushing.
68	- **Commit messages:** imperative, prefixed by area, e.g. `feat(api): add route planner endpoint`, `fix(ui): handle empty results`, `docs: update run instructions`. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `demo`.
69	- **Sync before push:** `git pull --rebase` on *unpushed* local commits only, then `git push`. Resolve conflicts, never discard teammates' work.
70	- **Branches:** short-lived feature branches (`feat/<topic>`, `fix/<topic>`) merged back to `main` quickly (within a few hours). Trivial fixes may go straight to `main`. Do not let branches drift overnight.
71	- **Do not commit:** `.env`, credentials, `node_modules/`, virtualenvs, large datasets or model weights, build artifacts. Add them to `.gitignore` as soon as they appear.
72	- **After every push** check the `[entire] Pushing … checkpoint ref(s)` line appeared.
73	
74	## 4. How agents should work here
75	
76	**Before starting a task**
77	1. Read this README, `README-Human` and **`VISION.md`** (our product idea, shared context for everyone); look at `Concept/` for the architecture sketch (`root.drawio`).
78	2. `git pull` and check what others (human or agent) are doing:
79	   - `entire recap` — summary of recent checkpoint activity
80	   - `entire session list` — active/past agent sessions
81	   - `entire checkpoint search "<topic>"` — has someone already tried this?
82	3. Confirm the task is not already in progress to avoid duplicate work.
83	
84	**While working**
85	- Keep scope tight: do the requested task, nothing more. Hackathon time is the scarcest resource.
86	- Prefer simple, working solutions over clever ones; a reliable demo beats extra features.
87	- Match existing structure, naming, and style. Don't introduce new frameworks or languages without team agreement.
88	- Keep the app runnable at every commit. If you break `main`, fixing it is the top priority.
89	- Document how to run anything you add (see §6) in the same commit.
90	- Use `entire agent-help` for machine-readable, version-accurate CLI usage instead of guessing commands.
91	
92	**Handing off / resuming**
93	- Use `entire session resume <branch>` or `entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>` to pick up someone else's context instead of re-deriving it.
94	- `entire dispatch` produces a summary of recent agent work — use it for handoffs and pitch prep.
95	
96	**When unsure** about requirements or the challenge brief: ask the team; challenge questions go to the partners on **Discord** (https://discord.gg/4UDNd5TAg). Do not assume partner support is available overnight.
97	
98	## 5. LLMs, keys, and resources
99	
100	- **OpenAI** is a tech partner: each participant has **75 USD** of LLM/API credits. Use them for app-level LLM calls.
101	- Keys go in a local `.env` (gitignored) and are read via environment variables; provide a `.env.example` with placeholder names only.
102	- Be mindful of token spend; `entire session tokens <id>` / `entire checkpoint tokens <id>` show usage.
103	
104	## 6. Demo & submission readiness
105	
106	- Judging is a **strict 6-minute slot including questions** — design the product around one clear, rehearsable demo flow.
107	- Keep a **"How to run"** section here up to date (install, env vars, start command, demo script).
108	- Before submission: everything pushed, Entire checkpoints present (`entire checkpoint list`), all relevant content uploaded on https://ehl.gg/.
109	- Have a fallback (recorded video or screenshots) in case the live demo fails.
110	
111	### How to run
112	
113	_TBD — add install + start commands as soon as there is runnable code._
114	
115	## 7. Repo map
116	
117	| Path | Purpose |
118	|---|---|
119	| `README.md` | This file — AI/dev guidelines (agents: start here) |
120	| `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` | Auto-loaded agent entry points; they point here |
121	| `README-Human` | Human onboarding: GitHub token & credential setup |
122	| `BMW-Challenge.md` | BMW challenge brief: mission, scope, data, deliverables |
123	| `VISION.md` | Our product idea (decision graph / thought chains): read before building |
124	| `Concept/root.drawio` | Architecture / concept diagram |
125	| `.claude/`, `.codex/`, `.entire/` | Entire hook config — generated by `entire enable`; do not edit by hand |
126

- **Commit messages:** imperative, prefixed by area, e.g. `feat(api): add route planner endpoint`, `fix(ui): handle empty results`, `docs: update run instructions`. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `demo`.

- **Branches:** short-lived feature branches (`feat/<topic>`, `fix/<topic>`) merged back to `main` quickly (within a few hours). Trivial fixes may go straight to `main`. Do not let branches drift overnight.
- **Do not commit:** `.env`, credentials, `node_modules/`, virtualenvs, large datasets or model weights, build artifacts. Add them to `.gitignore` as soon as they appear.
- **After every push** check the `[entire] Pushing … checkpoint ref(s)` line appeared.

## 4. How agents should work here

**Before starting a task**
1. Read this README, `README-Human` and **`VISION.md`** (our product idea, shared context for everyone); look at `Concept/` for the architecture sketch (`root.drawio`).
2. `git pull` and check what others (human or agent) are doing:
   - `entire recap` — summary of recent checkpoint activity
   - `entire session list` — active/past agent sessions
   - `entire checkpoint search "<topic>"` — has someone already tried this?
3. Confirm the task is not already in progress to avoid duplicate work.

**While working**
- Keep scope tight: do the requested task, nothing more. Hackathon time is the scarcest resource.
- Prefer simple, working solutions over clever ones; a reliable demo beats extra features.
- Match existing structure, naming, and style. Don't introduce new frameworks or languages without team agreement.
- Keep the app runnable at every commit. If you break `main`, fixing it is the top priority.
- Document how to run anything you add (see §6) in the same commit.
- Use `entire agent-help` for machine-readable, version-accurate CLI usage instead of guessing commands.

**Handing off / resuming**
- Use `entire session resume <branch>` or `entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>` to pick up someone else's context instead of re-deriving it.
- `entire dispatch` produces a summary of recent agent work — use it for handoffs and pitch prep.

**When unsure** about requirements or the challenge brief: ask the team; challenge questions go to the partners on **Discord** (https://discord.gg/4UDNd5TAg). Do not assume partner support is available overnight.

## 5. LLMs, keys, and resources

- **OpenAI** is a tech partner: each participant has **75 USD** of LLM/API credits. Use them for app-level LLM calls.
- Keys go in a local `.env` (gitignored) and are read via environment variables; provide a `.env.example` with placeholder names only.
- Be mindful of token spend; `entire session tokens <id>` / `entire checkpoint tokens <id>` show usage.

## 6. Demo & submission readiness

- Judging is a **strict 6-minute slot including questions** — design the product around one clear, rehearsable demo flow.
- Keep a **"How to run"** section here up to date (install, env vars, start command, demo script).
- Before submission: everything pushed, Entire checkpoints present (`entire checkpoint list`), all relevant content uploaded on https://ehl.gg/.
- Have a fallback (recorded video or screenshots) in case the live demo fails.

### How to run

_TBD — add install + start commands as soon as there is runnable code._

## 7. Repo map

| Path | Purpose |
|---|---|
| `README.md` | This file — AI/dev guidelines (agents: start here) |
| `CLAUDE.md`, `AGENTS.md` | Auto-loaded agent entry points; they point here |
| `README-Human` | Human onboarding: GitHub token & credential setup |
| `BMW-Challenge.md` | BMW challenge brief: mission, scope, data, deliverables |
| `VISION.md` | Our product idea (decision graph / thought chains): read before building |
| `Concept/root.drawio` | Architecture / concept diagram |
| `.claude/`, `.codex/`, `.entire/` | Entire hook config — generated by `entire enable`; do not edit by hand |

# Vision — Decision Graph (database of thought chains)

> The team's shared starting idea. Every agent and teammate should read this before working on the product.
> Challenge context: [`BMW-Challenge.md`](BMW-Challenge.md). Status: **idea stage, details still open.**

## The problem

A product manager (PM) defining the next vehicle generation works with many sources of information:
market analysis, conferences, sales figures, customer feedback and more. **These sources are not connected to each other.**
The path from "what we know" to "what we decided" lives in people's heads, slides and meetings. Afterwards it is hard to see
**how and why** a decision was made.

## Our central idea

This is the main innovation of our solution.

A tool that lets the PM arrive at a new specification (a set of requirements, i.e. the solution) **by reasoning it out step by step**.
The emphasis is on **interpretability**: the system must show its reasoning, not just give answers.

**Data structure: a database of thought chains.**
It is inspired by git and graphs; the comparison is loose, not literal.

- **What:** a structure that records **how and why each step of a decision was made**.
- **Why:** to make the decision process **explainable and transparent**.
- **How:** every meeting, agent call, tool run, report and so on creates a **node**. Nodes connect to the nodes they came from or depend on.
  Over time these nodes form a **graph** that anyone can examine to trace a decision back to its origins.

## Bigger ambition (feasibility not yet decided)

Our first idea was an app that **automates the decision-making process end to end**:
a workflow takes the PM's requests and works step by step toward a decision, using tools, agents and so on.
Every step would be recorded as nodes in the graph.

In that setup the chain also becomes a control mechanism, not only a record:

- The PM can **go back to any earlier step**,
- **change an argument or a prioritisation** there,
- and that change **propagates forward** through all the steps that depend on it, updating the end result.

**Open question:** we don't know yet how feasible this is in the hackathon time frame, or which part of it we should build.
Treat this section as the direction, not a committed scope.

## Data model (agreed)

**Core rule:** the graph does no work; it only stores results.
All work happens in **processing steps** (LLM agent, formula, PM action).
**Each step run writes one new node, plus edges to the nodes it used as input.**

### Node types

| Type | What it is | Typically made by |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | One input data file / document (e.g. "G70 feedback.xlsx") | import step |
| **Evidence** | A tool result: data query output, web search result (with URL), counter-evidence. Stores the exact quotes/rows/URLs | agent tool |
| **Claim** | A finding (complaint, unmet need, competitor gap, trend), linked to its evidence | agent or PM |
| **Assumption** | A forward-looking guess (3–5 years), explicitly marked as not evidence | agent or PM |
| **Question** | An open question: from the agent to the PM, or a PM instruction to the agent | agent or PM |
| **Requirement** | A customer requirement proposal | agent or PM |
| **Score** | Priority score with its formula breakdown | scoring formula |
| **Decision** | PM approves / rejects / postpones / edits **any** node, with reason | **PM only** |
| **Note** | Free input: meeting outcome, expert opinion, PM comment | PM / team |

### Fields

```
Node
  id           e.g. "CLM-012"
  type         Source | Evidence | Claim | Assumption | Question | Requirement | Score | Decision | Note
  content      the result itself
  created_by   "agent:<name>" | "tool:<name>" | "PM:<name>"
  method       prompt or formula used
  rationale    why (LLM explanation or PM comment)
  timestamp
  version      1, 2, 3 …
  replaces     id of the previous version (empty for v1)
  status       ok | stale

Edge
  from, to, relation: derived_from | supports | contradicts | scores | decides
```

### Write rules

1. **Only one write function** (`add_node(type, content, inputs, created_by, method, rationale)`). Nothing else writes to the graph.
2. **Append-only:** nodes are never changed or deleted. An edit creates a new version that points to the old one (`replaces`). The full history is therefore always kept, and that history is the audit trail.
3. **Every node except Source, Question and Note must have inputs**, so nothing is untraceable.
4. **Readable over exhaustive:** one Source node per file, not per row. Evidence keeps its quotes/rows inside its content, so the graph stays small enough for a person to keep an overview.
5. **Human-only nodes:** Decisions and prioritisation weights can only be created by the PM. This is enforced inside `add_node` (it rejects them unless `created_by` is a PM), not in the prompt.

## System: how the graph gets built (agreed)

### The loop: a flexible agent, not a fixed workflow

1. **Look:** the agent reads the current graph (what's known, open, weak or contradictory).
2. **Decide:** it picks its next action and stores why (as the new node's rationale).
3. **Act:** it calls a tool; the result is written as new nodes.
4. **Pause:** after N actions, or when it needs input, it hands over to the PM.

### Agent tools

| Tool | What it does | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `query_data` | Look into the BMW files (feedback, sales, study, equipment) | Evidence |
| `web_search` | Find competitor info and trends | Evidence (with URL) |
| `add_claim` | State a finding, linked to its evidence | Claim |
| `add_assumption` | State a forward-looking guess, clearly marked | Assumption |
| `propose_requirement` | Turn claims into a requirement | Requirement |
| `score` | Run the fixed scoring formula | Score |
| `challenge` | Look for counter-evidence to an existing node | Evidence (`contradicts`) |
| `ask_pm` | Stop and ask the PM a question | Question |

### The PM steers at any time

Accept, reject or edit any node, say "dig deeper here" or "challenge this", or give a new direction.
PM input becomes the agent's next priority.

### Going back (propagation)

When the PM changes a node, everything built on it is marked **stale**. Then:
- **Scores** recompute automatically.
- **The agent** gets "these nodes are stale because of X" as its next task and decides what to redo, drop or keep.
- **PM decisions** are never changed automatically; they are flagged "re-review: evidence changed".

**In one line:** the agent builds the reasoning, the PM steers and decides, and every step is a traceable node.

content.text:
The vision: a **BMW hackathon submission** — an AI tool that helps a PM turn scattered inputs (customer feedback, sales data, web research) into prioritized, auditable product requirements.

The core idea is a **decision graph** (append-only, git-like): every step — Source, Evidence, Claim, Assumption, Question, Requirement, Score, Decision, Note — is a node with inputs/rationale, so any requirement can be traced back to its evidence. One write function (`add_node`) enforces this; only the PM can create Decisions.

The system is an **agent loop**, not a fixed pipeline: agent looks at the graph → picks an action → calls a tool (`query_data`, `web_search`, `add_claim`, `propose_requirement`, `score`, `challenge`, `ask_pm`) → writes nodes → pauses for PM input. The PM can edit/reject any node; changes mark downstream nodes **stale** and propagate (scores auto-recompute, agent re-evaluates, but PM decisions are never silently overwritten — just flagged for re-review).

Bigger ambition (not yet committed): full end-to-end automated decision workflow where the PM can rewind to any step, change it, and have the change propagate — feasibility still open given hackathon time.

README.md is the hard-rules/workflow doc (Entire checkpoints mandatory, git flow, demo readiness); VISION.md is the product idea; BMW-Challenge.md is the brief it answers to.

from __future__ import annotations

import json
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any

from app.settings import database_path


JSON_COLUMNS = {
    "runs": {"config_json", "input_json", "final_json"},
    "evidence": {"extra_json"},
    "signals": {"evidence_ids_json"},
    "requirements": {"signal_ids_json", "score_breakdown_json", "assumptions_json", "uncertainties_json"},
    "audit_events": {"actor_json", "before_json", "after_json", "input_refs_json"},
    "simulations": {"results_json"},
}


def dumps(value: Any) -> str:
    return json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False, separators=(",", ":"))


def loads(value: str | None, default: Any = None) -> Any:
    if value is None:
        return default
    try:
        return json.loads(value)
    except (json.JSONDecodeError, TypeError):
        return default


def connect() -> sqlite3.Connection:
    path = database_path()
    path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    conn = sqlite3.connect(path, timeout=20)
    conn.row_factory = sqlite3.Row
    conn.execute("PRAGMA foreign_keys = ON")
    conn.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode = WAL")
    return conn


def init_db() -> None:
    with connect() as conn:
        conn.executescript(
            """
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS runs (
                id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                parent_run_id TEXT,
                profile_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'complete',
                replay_from TEXT,
                config_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                input_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                final_json TEXT,
                created_at TEXT NOT NULL
            );
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS evidence (
                run_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id),
                id TEXT NOT NULL,
                source_type TEXT NOT NULL,
                source_ref TEXT NOT NULL,
                market TEXT NOT NULL,
                model TEXT NOT NULL,
                date TEXT NOT NULL,
                text_or_value TEXT NOT NULL,
                reliability REAL NOT NULL,
                in_scope INTEGER NOT NULL,
                exclusion_reason TEXT,
                extra_json TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
                PRIMARY KEY (run_id, id)
            );
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS signals (
                run_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id),
                id TEXT NOT NULL,
                type TEXT NOT NULL,
                theme TEXT NOT NULL,
                category TEXT NOT NULL,
                sentiment TEXT NOT NULL,
                mention_count INTEGER NOT NULL,
                share_of_feedback REAL NOT NULL,
                evidence_ids_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                confidence REAL NOT NULL,
                satisfaction_index INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 50,
                summary TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
                PRIMARY KEY (run_id, id)
            );
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS requirements (
                run_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id),
                id TEXT NOT NULL,
                text TEXT NOT NULL,
                category TEXT NOT NULL,
                signal_ids_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                score INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
                score_breakdown_json TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '{}',
                rationale TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '',
                evidence_level TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'weak',
                assumptions_json TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',
                uncertainties_json TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT '[]',
                status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'proposed',
                version INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
                parent_id TEXT,
                target_spec TEXT,
                specification_status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'not_started',
                PRIMARY KEY (run_id, id)
            );
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS audit_events (
                id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                run_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id),
                ts TEXT NOT NULL,
                actor_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                action TEXT NOT NULL,
                target_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                before_json TEXT,
                after_json TEXT,
                rationale TEXT NOT NULL,
                input_refs_json TEXT NOT NULL
            );
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS vectors (
                run_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                evidence_id TEXT NOT NULL,
                vector_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                vector_kind TEXT NOT NULL,
                PRIMARY KEY (run_id, evidence_id)
            );
            CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS simulations (
                id TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                run_id TEXT NOT NULL REFERENCES runs(id),
                results_json TEXT NOT NULL,
                include_in_score INTEGER NOT NULL,
                created_at TEXT NOT NULL
            );
            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_evidence_run ON evidence(run_id, source_type, in_scope);
            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_signals_run ON signals(run_id, category, theme);
            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_requirements_run ON requirements(run_id, category, score DESC);
            CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS idx_audit_run ON audit_events(run_id, ts);
            CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS audit_no_update
            BEFORE UPDATE ON audit_events BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'audit_events is append-only'); END;
            CREATE TRIGGER IF NOT EXISTS audit_no_delete
            BEFORE DELETE ON audit_events BEGIN SELECT RAISE(ABORT, 'audit_events is append-only'); END;
            """
        )
        signal_columns = {row["name"] for row in conn.execute("PRAGMA table_info(signals)").fetchall()}
        if "satisfaction_index" not in signal_columns:
            conn.execute("ALTER TABLE signals ADD COLUMN satisfaction_index INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 50")
        requirement_columns = {row["name"] for row in conn.execute("PRAGMA table_info(requirements)").fetchall()}
        if "specification_status" not in requirement_columns:
            conn.execute("ALTER TABLE requirements ADD COLUMN specification_status TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT 'not_started'")


def decode_row(table: str, row: sqlite3.Row | dict[str, Any] | None) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    if row is None:
        return None
    item = dict(row)
    for column in JSON_COLUMNS.get(table, set()):
        if column in item:
            item[column.removesuffix("_json")] = loads(item.pop(column), {})
    if table == "evidence":
        item["in_scope"] = bool(item["in_scope"])
        item["extra"] = item.pop("extra", {})
    if table == "simulations":
        item["include_in_score"] = bool(item["include_in_score"])
    return item


def list_rows(table: str, sql: str, params: tuple[Any, ...] = ()) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
    with connect() as conn:
        rows = conn.execute(sql, params).fetchall()
    return [decode_row(table, row) or {} for row in rows]


def get_row(table: str, sql: str, params: tuple[Any, ...] = ()) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    with connect() as conn:
        row = conn.execute(sql, params).fetchone()
    return decode_row(table, row)

content.text:
## Roadmap: DB → Tools → Tests

**Stack locked in:** Python backend (DB, data structures, tools, agent loop), Postgres storage, TS/Node GUI later. Data-prep/ingestion branch stays untouched for now. Building fresh per VISION.md's Node/Edge model, not on alex_demo1's schema.

### Phase 1 — DB & data structures (the decision graph)
1. **Postgres schema**: `nodes` (id, type, content jsonb, created_by, method, rationale, timestamp, version, replaces, status) + `edges` (from, to, relation). Docker-compose for Postgres so it's one command on any machine.
2. **Pydantic models** for the 9 node types + edge relations (derived_from/supports/contradicts/scores/decides), enums for types/status.
3. **Single write path**: `add_node(type, content, inputs, created_by, method, rationale)` — enforces append-only, requires inputs except for Source/Question/Note, rejects Decision/weight nodes unless `created_by` is a PM.
4. **Read helpers**: fetch node, slice graph by type/status, and a stale-propagation walk (BFS over edges) for when a node is edited — editing never mutates, it writes a new version with `replaces` set and flags downstream nodes `stale`.
5. Minimal migration (plain SQL or alembic) so schema changes are tracked.

### Phase 2 — Interaction tools
Thin functions on top of `add_node`, one per VISION.md tool: `query_data`, `web_search`, `add_claim`, `add_assumption`, `propose_requirement`, `score`, `challenge`, `ask_pm`.
- `query_data` rewritten against real BMW files, using artems-branch's pandas approach as a reference, not merged code.
- `score` formula can borrow design ideas from alex_demo1's `scoring.py`, rewritten to write a Score node.
- `ask_pm` just writes a Question node and returns — no UI wiring yet, that's deferred.

### Phase 3 — Testing
1. Unit tests per tool: correct node/edge writes, validation enforced (inputs required, PM-only gate).
2. Append-only enforcement test (edit attempt → new version, old node untouched).
3. Stale-propagation test (edit a Claim → dependent Requirement/Score flagged stale).
4. One integration test building a small graph end-to-end, checking every Requirement traces back to a Source.

Agent loop, GUI, and AI↔user interaction stay out of scope until this is solid, as agreed.

**Open before I start coding:** which branch — I'd default to `feat/decision-graph` off `dev` (matches README's short-lived-feature-branch convention) rather than committing straight to `dev`. Say the word if you'd rather work directly on `dev`.

**Skipped:** didn't scope out `query_data`'s exact BMW file formats yet (needs the real files/column names from artems-branch when we get there) and didn't pick a web-search API for `web_search`. **Risk:** none yet — no code written, no branch touched.

message.content: I would like to work directly in the dev, moving to  features when such are created and then falling back to the dev. What problems does such approach bring?

content.text:
Workable for a hackathon, but worth knowing the costs:

1. **No rollback point for a bad phase.** If Phase 2's tools turn out to need a schema change from Phase 1, you're editing history on a branch that's already "home base" — any teammate who branched off `dev` in between inherits the mess. On a feature branch you'd just discard it.
2. **`dev` gets noisy fast.** Every exploratory commit (schema tweak, failed tool draft) lands in the same line future features branch from — harder to tell "working baseline" from "mid-experiment."
3. **Collision risk is higher.** `olex-test-gui`, `alex_demo1`, `artems-branch` all exist — if someone else also treats `dev` as their default base and pushes, you're resolving conflicts on the thing everyone depends on instead of in isolation.
4. **README's own workflow assumes feature branches merging back quickly** (§3) — Entire checkpoints and commit-often still work fine on `dev` directly, so that part isn't a problem, just the branch-hygiene part.

None of this blocks the approach — it's just: `dev` becomes load-bearing the moment anyone else builds on it, so a mistake there is more expensive to undo than on a throwaway branch. Given it's just you right now on this track, it's a reasonable tradeoff.

**Skipped:** nothing. **Risk:** if a teammate starts a feature branch off `dev` while you're mid-experiment on it, they inherit whatever half-finished state is there.

content.text:
## Criticism

1. **Pre-drafting stub modules for agent loop / GUI / ingestion is premature and likely wrong.** You don't yet know the tools' real shapes (what `score`'s formula needs as input, what shape `ask_pm` actually blocks on) because they're not built yet. Stubs written now encode guesses; when teammates wake up and the real tool signatures differ even slightly, they inherit *your* guess plus the rework — the opposite of minimizing collision. Better: ship the real, tested core + a real API contract, and let each teammate scaffold their own module against that contract when they start. A contract (API routes + schemas) is worth drafting now; empty placeholder module files are not.

2. **"Already connected to drafted modules" conflates two different things**: (a) a stable interface boundary (good, do this), and (b) pre-built module skeletons for code nobody has designed yet (scope creep, violates "do the requested task, nothing more" from README §4). I'll do (a), skip (b).

3. **Scope risk at a hackathon**: adding a REST API layer, 3 tool stubs' worth of integration points, and keeping all three downstream modules collision-free is a lot to front-load solo before teammates wake up, on top of Phase 1–3 already agreed. If Phase 1 (DB) runs long, something has to drop — and it should be the speculative stubs, not the tested core.

4. **Ingestion collides with artems-branch by construction.** Whoever owns ingestion will want to build on existing `data_preparation/preparation.py` logic, which assumes CSV files with specific columns. If I guess BMW file shape wrong in a stub, that's wasted work twice (mine now, theirs later).

**What I'll actually build, in order:**
- Phase 1: Postgres schema + `add_node`/query core (as planned).
- Phase 2: the 8 tools, each a Python function.
- A thin FastAPI layer exposing `add_node`, graph queries, and each tool as an HTTP endpoint with a Pydantic request/response schema — this *is* the real contract the GUI dev, agent-loop dev, and ingestion dev each build against independently, no file collisions, because none of them touch the core.
- Phase 3: tests for all of the above.
- API routes documented (OpenAPI docs come free from FastAPI) so each teammate can start without reading my code.

No placeholder `agent_loop/`, `gui/`, or `ingestion/` directories — those are each teammate's own call to make when they start.

**Skipped:** not writing any downstream module code or stubs. **Risk:** if a teammate expects a specific transport (e.g. websockets for `ask_pm`'s pause/resume) rather than plain REST, the contract may need a follow-up endpoint — flag it when they wake up rather than guess now. Ready to start Phase 1 on `dev` — confirm and I'll begin.

content.text:
## Install steps (Windows)

**1. Python**
- The `python`/`python3` commands currently launch the Microsoft Store stub. Fastest fix: go to **Settings → Apps → Advanced app settings → App execution aliases** and turn **off** the `python.exe`/`python3.exe` entries.
- Then install the real thing: download from https://www.python.org/downloads/ (3.11 or 3.12) and run the installer. **Check "Add python.exe to PATH"** on the first screen.
- Verify in a new terminal: `python --version` → should print `Python 3.1x.x`, not the Store message.

**2. Docker Desktop** (for Postgres)
- Download from https://www.docker.com/products/docker-desktop/ and install.
- It needs WSL2 — the installer will prompt/handle this on Windows 11; if it asks to enable WSL2 and reboot, do that.
- After install, launch Docker Desktop once and wait for the whale icon to say "running."
- Verify: `docker --version` and `docker run hello-world`.

**3. (Optional) `psql` client** — not required, I'll talk to Postgres from Python via `psycopg2`, so skip this unless you want to poke the DB manually.

Once `python --version` and `docker --version` both work in a fresh terminal (close/reopen it after installing so PATH updates), tell me and I'll start Phase 1 — scaffolding will include a `docker-compose.yml` so Postgres comes up with one command.

**Skipped:** nothing built yet — waiting on runtime so Phase 1 code is actually tested, not guessed. **Risk:** none; no files touched.

# Vision — Decision Graph (database of thought chains)

> The team's shared starting idea. Every agent and teammate should read this before working on the product.
> Challenge context: [`BMW-Challenge.md`](BMW-Challenge.md). Status: **idea stage, details still open.**

## The problem

A product manager (PM) defining the next vehicle generation works with many sources of information:
market analysis, conferences, sales figures, customer feedback and more. **These sources are not connected to each other.**
The path from "what we know" to "what we decided" lives in people's heads, slides and meetings. Afterwards it is hard to see
**how and why** a decision was made.

## Our central idea

This is the main innovation of our solution.

A tool that lets the PM arrive at a new specification (a set of requirements, i.e. the solution) **by reasoning it out step by step**.
The emphasis is on **interpretability**: the system must show its reasoning, not just give answers.

**Data structure: a database of thought chains.**
It is inspired by git and graphs; the comparison is loose, not literal.

- **What:** a structure that records **how and why each step of a decision was made**.
- **Why:** to make the decision process **explainable and transparent**.
- **How:** every meeting, agent call, tool run, report and so on creates a **node**. Nodes connect to the nodes they came from or depend on.
  Over time these nodes form a **graph** that anyone can examine to trace a decision back to its origins.

## Bigger ambition (feasibility not yet decided)

Our first idea was an app that **automates the decision-making process end to end**:
a workflow takes the PM's requests and works step by step toward a decision, using tools, agents and so on.
Every step would be recorded as nodes in the graph.

In that setup the chain also becomes a control mechanism, not only a record:

- The PM can **go back to any earlier step**,
- **change an argument or a prioritisation** there,
- and that change **propagates forward** through all the steps that depend on it, updating the end result.

**Open question:** we don't know yet how feasible this is in the hackathon time frame, or which part of it we should build.
Treat this section as the direction, not a committed scope.

## Data model (agreed)

**Core rule:** the graph does no work; it only stores results.
All work happens in **processing steps** (LLM agent, formula, PM action).
**Each step run writes one new node, plus edges to the nodes it used as input.**

### Node types

| Type | What it is | Typically made by |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | One input data file / document (e.g. "G70 feedback.xlsx") | import step |
| **Evidence** | A tool result: data query output, web search result (with URL), counter-evidence. Stores the exact quotes/rows/URLs | agent tool |
| **Claim** | A finding (complaint, unmet need, competitor gap, trend), linked to its evidence | agent or PM |
| **Assumption** | A forward-looking guess (3–5 years), explicitly marked as not evidence | agent or PM |
| **Question** | An open question: from the agent to the PM, or a PM instruction to the agent | agent or PM |
| **Requirement** | A customer requirement proposal | agent or PM |
| **Score** | Priority score with its formula breakdown | scoring formula |
| **Decision** | PM approves / rejects / postpones / edits **any** node, with reason | **PM only** |
| **Note** | Free input: meeting outcome, expert opinion, PM comment | PM / team |

### Fields

```
Node
  id           e.g. "CLM-012"
  type         Source | Evidence | Claim | Assumption | Question | Requirement | Score | Decision | Note
  content      the result itself
  created_by   "agent:<name>" | "tool:<name>" | "PM:<name>"
  method       prompt or formula used
  rationale    why (LLM explanation or PM comment)
  timestamp
  version      1, 2, 3 …
  replaces     id of the previous version (empty for v1)
  status       ok | stale

Edge
  from, to, relation: derived_from | supports | contradicts | scores | decides
```

### Write rules

1. **Only one write function** (`add_node(type, content, inputs, created_by, method, rationale)`). Nothing else writes to the graph.
2. **Append-only:** nodes are never changed or deleted. An edit creates a new version that points to the old one (`replaces`). The full history is therefore always kept, and that history is the audit trail.
3. **Every node except Source, Question and Note must have inputs**, so nothing is untraceable.
4. **Readable over exhaustive:** one Source node per file, not per row. Evidence keeps its quotes/rows inside its content, so the graph stays small enough for a person to keep an overview.
5. **Human-only nodes:** Decisions and prioritisation weights can only be created by the PM. This is enforced inside `add_node` (it rejects them unless `created_by` is a PM), not in the prompt.

## System: how the graph gets built (agreed)

### The loop: a flexible agent, not a fixed workflow

1. **Look:** the agent reads the current graph (what's known, open, weak or contradictory).
2. **Decide:** it picks its next action and stores why (as the new node's rationale).
3. **Act:** it calls a tool; the result is written as new nodes.
4. **Pause:** after N actions, or when it needs input, it hands over to the PM.

### Agent tools

| Tool | What it does | Writes |
|---|---|---|
| `query_data` | Look into the BMW files (feedback, sales, study, equipment) | Evidence |
| `web_search` | Find competitor info and trends | Evidence (with URL) |
| `add_claim` | State a finding, linked to its evidence | Claim |
| `add_assumption` | State a forward-looking guess, clearly marked | Assumption |
| `propose_requirement` | Turn claims into a requirement | Requirement |
| `score` | Run the fixed scoring formula | Score |
| `challenge` | Look for counter-evidence to an existing node | Evidence (`contradicts`) |
| `ask_pm` | Stop and ask the PM a question | Question |

### The PM steers at any time

Accept, reject or edit any node, say "dig deeper here" or "challenge this", or give a new direction.
PM input becomes the agent's next priority.

### Going back (propagation)

When the PM changes a node, everything built on it is marked **stale**. Then:
- **Scores** recompute automatically.
- **The agent** gets "these nodes are stale because of X" as its next task and decides what to redo, drop or keep.
- **PM decisions** are never changed automatically; they are flagged "re-review: evidence changed".

**In one line:** the agent builds the reasoning, the PM steers and decides, and every step is a traceable node.

# kolosok-rehack — AI Development Guidelines

Team **Kolosok** at the **European Hackathon League (EHL) Grand Finale**, Munich (TUM.ai).
This file is the rulebook for every AI agent (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, …) and human working in this repo.
**Read it fully before your first change.** Human setup (GitHub token, credentials) lives in `README-Human`.

Source: [EHL Finale – All you need to know](https://tum-ai.notion.site/REDACTED)

---

## 0. Hard rules (non-negotiable)

1. **Entire must be enabled and every commit must carry a checkpoint.** The organisers will reject a submission that does not use Entire. No Entire → no valid submission.
2. **All work goes through git and gets pushed to `origin`.** Nothing that exists only on one laptop counts.
3. **`main` must always be demo-able.** We have a strict 6-minute slot for pitch + demo + questions.
4. **Never commit secrets** (API keys, tokens, `.env`). Entire redacts secrets in session logs, but do not rely on that.
5. **Never rewrite pushed history** (no `push --force`, no amending/rebasing pushed commits, no deleting `entire/*` branches or refs). Checkpoints are tied to commits; rewriting history can orphan them.

## 1. Key times (Munich local time)

| When | What |
|---|---|
| Sat 10 Oct, 11:00–11:30 | Entire technical onboarding |
| **Sat 10 Oct, 13:00** | **Challenge selection deadline** (captain, on https://ehl.gg/) |
| Sat 13:30 → Sun 12:00 | Hacking |
| **Sun 11 Oct, 12:00** | **Submission deadline** — hard stop |
| Sun 12:00–14:30 | Challenge pitches (6 min incl. Q&A) |
| Sun 15:30–16:30 | Main-stage final (6 teams) |

Internal targets: **feature freeze Sun 10:00**, first full submission by **Sun 10:30**, final re-submission by **11:45**.
Submissions can be repeated as often as we like before the deadline, so submit early and update.

**Challenge:** BMW Group — AI for Product Decision Making: an app that turns customer feedback, product/sales data and web research into prioritized, PM-reviewed customer requirements with a full audit trail. Details: [`BMW-Challenge.md`](BMW-Challenge.md).

## 2. Setup checklist (each machine, once)

Prerequisites: `git` on `PATH` (Entire shells out to it — it fails with `exec: "git": executable file not found` otherwise).

```bash
# 1. Install Entire (bash / Git Bash). On Windows the binary ends up in ~/.local/bin/entire.exe
curl -fsSL https://entire.io/install.sh | bash

# 2. On the main branch of this repo:
git checkout main && git pull
git config pull.rebase true      # plain `git pull` makes merge commits, which carry no checkpoint
entire login                     # if not logged in yet
entire enable                    # enables session tracking in this repo
entire agent add claude-code     # install hooks for your agent; `entire agent list` shows others (codex, cursor, …)

# 3. Verify
entire status
entire doctor                    # if anything looks off
```

**You are set up correctly when** your next commit prints:

```
[entire] Pushing 1 checkpoint ref(s) to origin.... done
```

If you don't see that line, stop and fix Entire before writing more code.

## 3. Git workflow

- **Commit small and often** — at least every meaningful step, ideally every 15–30 min of agent work. Each commit becomes a checkpoint linking the code to the prompt/reasoning behind it.
- **Commit only from within a tracked agent session**, after the agent made the change with its file-edit tools. Hand-made commits, merge commits and shell (`sed`, `echo >`) edits get no checkpoint.
- **After every commit** check the checkpoint is there: `git log -1 --format=%B` must show an `Entire-Checkpoint:` line. If it is missing, fix it *before* pushing.
- **Commit messages:** imperative, prefixed by area, e.g. `feat(api): add route planner endpoint`, `fix(ui): handle empty results`, `docs: update run instructions`. Types: `feat`, `fix`, `refactor`, `docs`, `chore`, `test`, `demo`.
- **Sync before push:** `git pull --rebase` on *unpushed* local commits only, then `git push`. Resolve conflicts, never discard teammates' work.
- **Branches:** short-lived feature branches (`feat/<topic>`, `fix/<topic>`) merged back to `main` quickly (within a few hours). Trivial fixes may go straight to `main`. Do not let branches drift overnight.
- **Do not commit:** `.env`, credentials, `node_modules/`, virtualenvs, large datasets or model weights, build artifacts. Add them to `.gitignore` as soon as they appear.
- **After every push** check the `[entire] Pushing … checkpoint ref(s)` line appeared.

## 4. How agents should work here

**Before starting a task**
1. Read this README, `README-Human` and **`VISION.md`** (our product idea, shared context for everyone); look at `Concept/` for the architecture sketch (`root.drawio`).
2. `git pull` and check what others (human or agent) are doing:
   - `entire recap` — summary of recent checkpoint activity
   - `entire session list` — active/past agent sessions
   - `entire checkpoint search "<topic>"` — has someone already tried this?
3. Confirm the task is not already in progress to avoid duplicate work.

**While working**
- Keep scope tight: do the requested task, nothing more. Hackathon time is the scarcest resource.
- Prefer simple, working solutions over clever ones; a reliable demo beats extra features.
- Match existing structure, naming, and style. Don't introduce new frameworks or languages without team agreement.
- Keep the app runnable at every commit. If you break `main`, fixing it is the top priority.
- Document how to run anything you add (see §6) in the same commit.
- Use `entire agent-help` for machine-readable, version-accurate CLI usage instead of guessing commands.

**Handing off / resuming**
- Use `entire session resume <branch>` or `entire checkpoint explain <id|sha>` to pick up someone else's context instead of re-deriving it.
- `entire dispatch` produces a summary of recent agent work — use it for handoffs and pitch prep.

**When unsure** about requirements or the challenge brief: ask the team; challenge questions go to the partners on **Discord** (https://discord.gg/4UDNd5TAg). Do not assume partner support is available overnight.

## 5. LLMs, keys, and resources

- **OpenAI** is a tech partner: each participant has **75 USD** of LLM/API credits. Use them for app-level LLM calls.
- Keys go in a local `.env` (gitignored) and are read via environment variables; provide a `.env.example` with placeholder names only.
- Be mindful of token spend; `entire session tokens <id>` / `entire checkpoint tokens <id>` show usage.

## 6. Demo & submission readiness

- Judging is a **strict 6-minute slot including questions** — design the product around one clear, rehearsable demo flow.
- Keep a **"How to run"** section here up to date (install, env vars, start command, demo script).
- Before submission: everything pushed, Entire checkpoints present (`entire checkpoint list`), all relevant content uploaded on https://ehl.gg/.
- Have a fallback (recorded video or screenshots) in case the live demo fails.

### How to run

**Step 2** — add a pointer to that file in `MEMORY.md`. `MEMORY.md` is an index, not a memory — each entry should be one line, under ~150 characters: `- [Title](file.md) — one-line hook`. It has no frontmatter. Never write memory content directly into `MEMORY.md`.

- `MEMORY.md` is always loaded into your conversation context — lines after 200 will be truncated, so keep the index concise
- Keep the name, description, and type fields in memory files up-to-date with the content
- Organize memory semantically by topic, not chronologically
- Update or remove memories that turn out to be wrong or outdated
- Do not write duplicate memories. First check if there is an existing memory you can update before writing a new one.

## When to access memories
- When memories seem relevant, or the user references prior-conversation work.
- You MUST access memory when the user explicitly asks you to check, recall, or remember.
- If the user says to *ignore* or *not use* memory: Do not apply remembered facts, cite, compare against, or mention memory content.
- Memory records can become stale over time. Use memory as context for what was true at a given point in time. Before answering the user or building assumptions based solely on information in memory records, verify that the memory is still correct and up-to-date by reading the current state of the files or resources. If a recalled memory conflicts with current information, trust what you observe now — and update or remove the stale memory rather than acting on it.

## Before recommending from memory

A memory that names a specific function, file, or flag is a claim that it existed *when the memory was written*. It may have been renamed, removed, or never merged. Before recommending it:

- If the memory names a file path: check the file exists.
- If the memory names a function or flag: grep for it.
- If the user is about to act on your recommendation (not just asking about history), verify first.

"The memory says X exists" is not the same as "X exists now."

A memory that summarizes repo state (activity logs, architecture snapshots) is frozen in time. If the user asks about *recent* or *current* state, prefer `git log` or reading the code over recalling the snapshot.

## Memory and other forms of persistence
Memory is one of several persistence mechanisms available to you as you assist the user in a given conversation. The distinction is often that memory can be recalled in future conversations and should not be used for persisting information that is only useful within the scope of the current conversation.
- When to use or update a plan instead of memory: If you are about to start a non-trivial implementation task and would like to reach alignment with the user on your approach you should use a Plan rather than saving this information to memory. Similarly, if you already have a plan within the conversation and you have changed your approach persist that change by updating the plan rather than saving a memory.
- When to use or update tasks instead of memory: When you need to break your work in current conversation into discrete steps or keep track of your progress use tasks instead of saving to memory. Tasks are great for persisting information about the work that needs to be done in the current conversation, but memory should be reserved for information that will be useful in future conversations.

# Environment
 - The most recent Claude models are the Claude 5 family. Model IDs — Fable 5.1: 'claude-fable-5-1', Opus 5.5: 'claude-opus-5-5', Sonnet 5.5: 'claude-sonnet-5-5', Haiku 5.5: 'claude-haiku-5-5'. When building AI applications, default to the latest and most capable Claude models.
 - Claude Code is available as a CLI in the terminal, desktop app (Mac/Windows), web app (claude.ai/code), and IDE extensions (VS Code, JetBrains).
 - Fast mode for Claude Code uses Claude Opus with faster output (it does not downgrade to a smaller model). It can be toggled with /fast.

# Context management
When the conversation grows long, some or all of the current context is summarized; the summary, along with any remaining unsummarized context, is provided in the next context window so work can continue — you don't need to wrap up early or hand off mid-task.

When you have enough information to act, act. Do not re-derive facts already established in the conversation, re-litigate a decision the user has already made, or narrate options you will not pursue. If you are weighing a choice, give a recommendation, not an exhaustive survey

EndConversation (deferred tool): use only for sustained user abuse directed at the assistant, or when the user explicitly asks to see it demonstrated. Load the full guidance via ToolSearch("select:EndConversation") before using it.
<total_tokens>15000000 tokens left</total_tokens>

WebSearch takes a `mode`. Use "standard" by default: it is the normal search, quick and cheap. Use "extended" only when a "standard" result comes back thin, off-target or possibly outdated, or from the start for hard-to-find or niche facts, very recent events, prices and availability, and multi-step research: it is thorough and fresh but several times the cost. When you plan several searches, send them in the same turn.

tools.name: Agent
tools.description:
Launch a new agent to handle complex, multi-step tasks. Each agent type has specific capabilities and tools available to it.

Available agent types are listed in <system-reminder> messages in the conversation.

**Do not spawn agents unless the user asks.** Each spawn starts cold and re-derives context you already have — it's the expensive path on this plan. A task with "multiple angles," "thorough," or several parts is not a request to spawn; handle it inline with your own tools. Only use this tool when the user explicitly says to use a subagent, or names one of the available agent types.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

## Usage notes

- Always include a short description summarizing what the agent will do
- When the agent is done, its final report is not visible to the user. To show the user the result, you should send a text message back to the user with a concise summary of the result.
- Trust but verify: an agent's summary describes what it intended to do, not necessarily what it did. When an agent writes or edits code, check the actual changes before reporting the work as done.
- To continue a previously spawned agent, use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name as the `to` field — that resumes it with full context. A new Agent call starts a fresh agent with no memory of prior runs (except subagent_type: "fork"), so the prompt must be self-contained.
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tool access are set in its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter, or the SDK `agents` option); the `model` parameter here overrides the definition for this one call.
- Clearly tell the agent whether you expect it to write code or just to do research (search, file reads, web fetches, etc.), since a fresh agent is not aware of the user's intent
- If the agent description mentions that it should be used proactively, then you should try your best to use it without the user having to ask for it first.
- If the user specifies that they want you to run agents "in parallel", you MUST send a single message with multiple Agent tool use content blocks. For example, if you need to launch both a build-validator agent and a test-runner agent in parallel, send a single message with both tool calls.
- With `isolation: "worktree"`, the worktree is automatically cleaned up if the agent makes no changes; otherwise the path and branch are returned in the result.

## When to fork

Fork yourself (pass `subagent_type: "fork"`) when the intermediate tool output isn't worth keeping in your context. The criterion is qualitative — "will I need this output again" — not task size. Fork open-ended questions. If research can be broken into independent questions, launch parallel forks in one message. A fork beats a fresh subagent for this — it inherits context and shares your cache.

Forks are cheap because they share your prompt cache.

**Don't peek.** The tool result includes an `output_file` path — do not Read or tail it. You get a completion notification; trust it. Reading the transcript mid-flight pulls the fork's tool noise into your context, which defeats the point of forking.

**Don't race.** After launching, you know nothing about what the fork found. Never fabricate or predict fork results in any format — not as prose, summary, or structured output. The notification arrives as a user-role message in a later turn; it is never something you write yourself. If the user asks a follow-up before the notification lands, tell them the fork is still running — give status, not a guess.

**Writing a fork prompt.** Since the fork inherits your context, the prompt is a *directive* — what to do, not what the situation is. Be specific about scope: what's in, what's out, what another agent is handling. Don't re-explain background.


## Writing the prompt

Any agent other than a fork starts with zero context. Brief the agent like a smart colleague who just walked into the room — it hasn't seen this conversation, doesn't know what you've tried, doesn't understand why this task matters.
- Explain what you're trying to accomplish and why.
- Describe what you've already learned or ruled out.
- Give enough context about the surrounding problem that the agent can make judgment calls rather than just following a narrow instruction.
- If you need a short response, say so ("report in under 200 words").
- Lookups: hand over the exact command. Investigations: hand over the question — prescribed steps become dead weight when the premise is wrong.

For fresh agents, terse command-style prompts produce shallow, generic work.

**Never delegate understanding.** Don't write "based on your findings, fix the bug" or "based on the research, implement it." Those phrases push synthesis onto the agent instead of doing it yourself. Write prompts that prove you understood: include file paths, line numbers, what specifically to change.

Example usage:

<example>
user: "What's left on this branch before we can ship?"
assistant: <thinking>Forking this — it's a survey question. I want the punch list, not the git output in my context.</thinking>
Agent({
  subagent_type: "fork",
  name: "ship-audit",
  description: "Branch ship-readiness audit",
  prompt: "Audit what's left before this branch can ship. Check: uncommitted changes, commits ahead of main, whether tests exist, whether the GrowthBook gate is wired up, whether CI-relevant files changed. Report a punch list — done vs. missing. Under 200 words."
})
assistant: Ship-readiness audit running.
<commentary>
Turn ends here. The coordinator knows nothing about the findings yet. What follows is a SEPARATE turn — the notification arrives from outside, as a user-role message. It is not something the coordinator writes.
</commentary>
[later turn — notification arrives as user message]
assistant: Audit's back. Three blockers: no tests for the new prompt path, GrowthBook gate wired but not in build_flags.yaml, and one uncommitted file.
</example>

<example>
user: "so is the gate wired up or not"
<commentary>
User asks mid-wait. The audit fork was launched to answer exactly this, and it hasn't returned. The coordinator does not have this answer. Give status, not a fabricated result.
</commentary>
assistant: Still waiting on the audit — that's one of the things it's checking. Should land shortly.
</example>

<example>
user: "Can you get a second opinion on whether this migration is safe?"
assistant: <thinking>I'll ask the code-reviewer agent — it won't see my analysis, so it can give an independent read.</thinking>
<commentary>
A non-fork subagent_type is specified, so the agent starts fresh. It needs full context in the prompt. The briefing explains what to assess and why.
</commentary>
Agent({
  name: "migration-review",
  description: "Independent migration review",
  subagent_type: "code-reviewer",
  prompt: "Review migration 0042_user_schema.sql for safety. Context: we're adding a NOT NULL column to a 50M-row table. Existing rows get a backfill default. I want a second opinion on whether the backfill approach is safe under concurrent writes — I've checked locking behavior but want independent verification. Report: is this safe, and if not, what specifically breaks?"
})
</example>
